items.title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
items.excerpt: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said. items.title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
items.excerpt: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters. At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors. Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads. Read full article Comments

items.title: Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now
items.excerpt: A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull. Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5) , indicating a "moderate" brain injury, just one point above "mild." He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5). In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head. items.title: Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump
items.excerpt: Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes. The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times . Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region. Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region's undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. items.excerpt: # agent-browser Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell. agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. `snapshot` returns the page as compact text with a ref such as `@e1` for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call. ## Install ```bash npm install -g agent-browser agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only) ``` - **Homebrew:** `brew install agent-browser`, then `agent-browser install`. - **Linux:** `agent-browser install --with-deps` also installs the browser's system libraries. - **No install:** `npx agent-browser open example.com`. Project installs, building from source, `upgrade`, and `doctor` are covered in [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/installation). ## Quick start ```bash agent-browser open example.com agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-browser get url # check the result agent-browser close ``` The snapshot for `example.com`: ``` - link "Learn more" [ref=e1] ``` - Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again. - CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example…

items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. items.title: Your Coding Agent Can't Undo Its Own Mistakes - Tanmay Sah & Dolly Sah
items.excerpt: Tanmay Sah and Dolly Sah look at a capability today's coding agents are missing: undoing what they've done. Drawing on their research projects UndoBench and EvoUndo, they show that an agent that completes a task can't necessarily put things back when something breaks, because Git doesn't cover external API calls, runtime config or notifications, and retrying doesn't reverse side effects. In EvoUndo, 197 of 478 changes that made an agent more capable (about 42%) also broke its ability to recover. They lay out an approach that captures the original state, picks the right response (retry, restore, compensate or escalate) and independently verifies the result. Tanmay Sah https://x.com/TanmayGradient Dolly Sah Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.title: Your Company Has No Model of Itself. Agents Can Build One - Joao Wenzel, Citadel Securities
items.excerpt: Every company has someone who knows everything: the reorgs, the politics, which projects are really on track. Joao Wenzel of Citadel Securities explains how his team approximates that person with an agentic system that builds an institutional memory from decks, Slack, meeting notes, code changes and agent traces. Borrowing the idea of a state estimator from robotics, the system updates its beliefs as evidence arrives, lets facts age, grades its own predictions against what actually happened, and takes corrections from people. He shows why simple retrieval isn't enough, how agents catch "watermelon projects" that are green on the outside and red on the inside, and how back-testing showed that projects the agent flagged were twice as likely to slip. items.title: SaaS is dead?
items.excerpt: In this solo episode, I explain why I say SaaS is dead and what I see taking its place. For 15 years, SaaS meant paying engineers to build a tool and charging per seat, and now models like Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Argon make the tool easy to build. I walk through what I call smart SaaS: give the tool away for free, collect data and network effects, and make money by upselling AI agents and human services. I share a calorie tracking example, three ways to charge, and why enterprises still pay per seat. If you build software, this episode gives you a map for building something people want in a market where the tool is free. Timestamps 00:00 – Intro 00:47 – SaaS 1.0 02:56 – SaaS 2.0: The New Business Model 05:12 – How to monetize SaaS 2.0 06:18 – Service is the new Software 07:22 – SaaS Is Dead, Long Live SaaS 08:58 – SMB vs Enterprise 10:31 – Closing Thoughts Key Points • AI makes the tool easy to build, so the per-seat model of the last 15 years has run its course. • Smart SaaS gives the tool away and collects data and network effects as payment. • The money comes from upselling intelligence from AI agents and services from humans. • Agents can charge by token or by outcome, and human services by the week or month. • SaaS for SMBs, prosumers, and individuals trends toward free, while enterprises still pay something per seat. • The market for getting things done is bigger than the market for tools, so the total market for SaaS grows. Democrats won the House and the Senate, flipped governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, and data-center restrictions passed in towns across the country. Goldman Sachs warns that 45% of planned US data-center capacity could be affected, and Texas alone is about a quarter of it. Ejaaz breaks down why an AI bull thinks the slowdown might actually be good for AI: no overbuild, data centers that pay their own way, and a race that rewards whoever uses compute most efficiently. We also cover why voters turned on data centers (power, land and water), Gina Hinojosa's conditions in Texas, the water myth, the market's split reaction (stocks up, AI stocks down, Elon's companies hit hardest), the 10 to 15 gigawatts that may not come online, the new stakeholder in the AI money loop, and what it means for the race with China. == FOLLOW EJAAZ ON TWITTER: https://x.com/cryptopunk7213 == Timestamps 00:00 America Hits Pause on AI 01:34 Power, Land and Water 02:38 Why Voters Turned 04:18 What the Midterms Changed 05:08 Texas Wants Data Centers to Pay 07:07 A Bipartisan Backlash 07:29 The China Problem 08:34 The Water Myth 09:55 Who Pays for Power 10:39 The Market Reaction 12:06 A New Stakeholder 13:07 Good News for the Bears 14:19 Stocks From Here 15:34 Efficiency Wins 17:24 AI Gets More Expensive 18:03 US vs China 19:51 Final Thoughts #ai #datacenters #midterms #elections #elonmusk == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade…

items.title: Elon Might End Grok Bot
items.excerpt: Over the weekend, Elon Musk told a Grok Bot user that "the cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," and usage limits tightened for hundreds of thousands of paying users. Three days earlier he'd pointed out that Grok Bot has no free tier, and two weeks before that he said he'd never seen anything grow as fast. Ejaaz breaks down what's actually going on: SpaceX can rent the same GPUs to Anthropic, which pays $1.25 billion a month today and about $3.1 billion a month from December, while Grok Bot's hardest tasks run on Anthropic's own Claude Opus 5.5. We also cover Grok Bot's rise to 600,000 daily users, the delays on Grok 4.8, the $60 billion Cursor acquisition, the trade-off between renting compute and running his own AI agent, the bear and bull case, and whether this is the first sign that AI is too expensive to sell at today's prices. == FOLLOW EJAAZ ON TWITTER: https://x.com/cryptopunk7213 == Timestamps 00:00 Elon's Grok Bot Problem 01:51 What Grok Bot Is 03:48 How Grok Bot Took Off 04:47 Grok's Model Problem 06:18 The Contradiction 06:58 The Landlord and the Tenant 08:35 The $60 Billion Cursor Bet 09:53 Rent the Chips or Run the Bot? 10:50 Why AI Agents Matter 12:46 Limits, Not a Shutdown 14:01 The Bear Case 17:46 The Bull Case 19:15 Final Thoughts #elonmusk #grok #spacex #anthropic #ai == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade Investment Platform Built for Everyday Investors. 👉…

items.title: We Need to Talk About Anthropic
items.excerpt: Last week, Anthropic's S-1 showed a company that was finally making money. Today's amended filing adds the third quarter, and that profit is gone: revenue jumped to nearly $17 billion, up 47% in three months, but Anthropic swung to a $567 million operating loss, and it disclosed $895 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, about $70 billion of it due in the next 12 months. Ejaaz breaks down why: demand outran the compute Anthropic had booked, so it paid up for $5 billion of short-term compute to keep serving customers. We also cover the $2 billion donation-matching charge, where the $895 billion is going (SpaceX, Google, Amazon, Broadcom and the neoclouds), whether Anthropic can pay for it, OpenAI's cut-down fundraise and the junk-rating worry, and the bull and bear case for the Anthropic IPO. == FOLLOW EJAAZ ON TWITTER: https://x.com/cryptopunk7213 == Timestamps 00:00 Anthropic's Profit Is Gone 01:50 Catching Up on the S-1 04:28 The Q3 Numbers 05:24 Three Reasons for the Loss 06:54 The Restaurant Analogy 07:56 The $2 Billion Donation Match 09:19 The $895 Billion Bill 12:32 Where the Money Goes 14:18 Can Anthropic Pay for It? 16:38 Less Than 0.1% of Budgets 17:48 Is the IPO a Buy or a Sell? 22:14 Final Thoughts #anthropic #claude #ipo #ai #stocks == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade Investment Platform Built for Everyday Investors. 👉 https://finance.yahoo.com/about/promos/gold/alphaspace/?ncid=100003571

items.title: Big Tech Just Bet Everything on the AI Crash
items.excerpt: AI stocks just had a brutal week. Google lost more than $500 billion in market value, Amazon fell 12% after hours on its earnings, and Intel had its worst day since 1974, all while the biggest tech companies reported record cloud revenue and promised to spend even more on AI next year. So is this the dot-com bubble all over again? Ejaaz walks through how the selloff started, why search and the open web are cracking, and who is really paying for the AI buildout. We also lay out the bear case (concentration, borrowing, VC-subsidized spending and the walls going up around Reddit and Amazon) and the bull case (real demand, cash-rich hyperscalers, labs with money in the bank, and what happened to the internet after 2000), and why this looks more like a correction than a collapse. == FOLLOW EJAAZ ON TWITTER: https://x.com/cryptopunk7213 == Timestamps 00:00 Is the AI Bubble Popping? 00:55 Big Tech Doubles Down 02:14 How the Selloff Started 03:11 Three Signals From Earnings 04:07 Search Is Breaking 04:59 Reddit Builds a Wall 07:20 The Overbuild Question 09:00 Who's Paying for It 10:13 Walls Around the Web 10:54 Amazon Blocks Meta's Muse 12:34 The Bear Case 13:46 The Bull Case 17:23 The Internet Still Won 18:51 Final Thoughts #ai #stocks #bubble #nvidia #google == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade Investment Platform Built for Everyday Investors. 👉 https://finance.yahoo.com/about/promos/gold/alphaspace/?ncid=100003571

items.title: Every User, Every Asset: The 10-Year Plan | Vibhu Norby, Solana Foundation Chief Product Officer
items.excerpt: Solana Foundation CPO Vibhu says Solana is a venture bet, and that onchain finance isn't even 0.1% of the way there: "I think the strategy of Solana is a little different from others. I think it is more of a venture strategy. And actually, if you talk to asset allocators, there's a great Bitwise report that came out recently where they interviewed a lot of allocators and they put Solana in a venture technology bet portion of their portfolio, in my opinion, very early. And we're very focused on market share. We think that where we are today versus where we're going to be in 10 years is literally one one thousandth of the trading volume and the TVL and all those kind of things. This is not just conjecture. If you just add up all the assets that exist onchain, you compare it to what's in the real world. We're not even point one percent the way there." — Vibhu Norby, CPO of the Solana Foundation on @TheRollupCo with Robbie Klages

Show HN: ChainBounty – improving the blockchain funding model
items.excerpt: Abstract. Token-funded bounties to incentivize competition-style participation in blockchain development projects would result in wider and better allocation of investment, and allow investors to diversify exposure across a field of potentially successful projects. Overall this would increase the rate of progress within development of the blockchain space. We propose a centralised platform for the administration of token-funded bounty driven development projects whereby experts allocate pools of invested capital according to the technical merits of development projects, and investors are rewarded with token allocation in funded projects. Draft Whitepaper: http://chainbounty.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/chainbount... We see this as bringing a variation of the YC model to blockchain - experts select large numbers of small projects and provide them with funding to reach the next level of development. This is in contrast to heavily funded ICOs where tiny teams of developers are given hundreds of millions of dollars. After feedback from HN readers: - Do you think this model will better incentivize development in the blockchain space? - What particular challenges do you think would be useful to run? https://twitter.com/ChainBounty/ https://www.facebook.com/ChainBounty-449553402088106/

items.title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
items.excerpt: I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later. Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context . I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll probably be Substack only ; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. This Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate. Take-off Speed from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me : Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.) At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse”…

items.title: Near Horizons
items.excerpt: Image by Claude Opus 5.5 using Python (NumPy and Pillow) This is written in my free time and personal capacity. Two Frames In AI safety, there are a couple of tensions at the heart of the field, which are interrelated. [1] Talent: we are talent-constrained and must recruit. But jobs and fellowships turn away nearly everyone. [2] Field size: we must expand the field and bring more people in. But the field is flooded with slop papers in conferences. And, most papers have a small audience, and aim to shift the practices of roughly five labs (and usually some subteam within them). [3] Status: we must avoid seeking status, as it disorients, corrupts. But, we must make the field legible and attractive to outsiders. Raising the bots: we must deceive the AIs to control them and evaluate them without confounds, obscuring what they know about their own situation. But, we hope to gain their trust, must rely on them to do good work at pace, shape their character and retain good relations. Speed: we must research in a slow mode, think deeply about the most important problem, do things to aim at high assurance. But it is crunch time. It was crunch time two months ago. We must make hacky progress now and trust that scale will clarify things later. I think these tensions are, at least in part, rooted in what I will call a "war" frame and a "civilisation" frame. These frames are oriented around a different end goal, or telos of AI safety. In the war frame, AI safety is a campaign with a…

items.title: Rhythm Stage Setup v5
items.excerpt: I recently finished the largest set of changes I've made to my rhythm stage setup in 4.5y . The basic interface is similar, but I have a lot more flexibility, more control, more options, and it's easier to travel with. My favorite part is the speech recognition for calling chords. I started off playing mandolin and piano, and then over the years added progressively more expressive footdrums . I added a breath controller . I built out a complex but expressive system where these different interfaces could interact to let me produce a coherent rhythm section . After a frustrating experience moving from one Mac to another and wanting to simplify, I moved from the Mac to a Raspberry Pi , set it all up as a pedalboard , and then again as a lighter pedalboard . During the last year and a bit, however, I haven't been tinkering. It did what I wanted, in a reliable and portable fashion. And it was hard to modify: the pedalboard was static, and the Raspberry Pi code wasn't easy to get at either. Which was fine, and probably good for me! I just played a lot of gigs (23 Kingfisher , 3 Free Raisins , 3 Dandelion ) and got better at it. But then it started breaking. My whistle synth box didn't always come up, the drums sometimes needed an external DI, and a USB sound card snapped. Flying back from Atlanta my gear suffered rough enough treatment to bend a USB B connector, and it was clear my system needed some love. I started with the most urgent portion: the whistle synth. items.title: What do LLMs Really Learn About Model Weights? A Stratification Approach to Examine Weight Space Programming
items.excerpt: TLDR I attempted to replicate “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” by Takehi et al (2026) with stratification on two reasoning models, GPT 6 Astra and Deepseek-V4.1-Flash. The task for the LLMs is to identify the game a ML model is trained for giving the weight of the model (using exact same prompt and weight defined by Takehi). Although both of these models do well on the surface (4/4 correct for Astra and 3/4 correct for Flash), the stratification approach exposes the difference in mechanism between these two models in approaching the problem. The experiment result shows that Flash depends a lot on channel label for the answer (while Astra's performance does not degrade when channel label does not present). Additionally, Astra is able to identify the game with good accuracy using only the first layer of weight or as few as 1000 weight values selected at random out of 17253 weight values (Flash's performance degrade substantially on these). So Astra survives this first round of stratification tests just for now. Comparing the results between Astra and Flash, it is obvious that Flash is relying heavily on prompt metadata instead of reading the weights. Background On November 2 an article “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” was published by Takehi et al (2026). The article is cleanly written and one of the claims is that by looking at model weights, GPT 6 Astra can tell what the model is trained to do. The article reports that Astra is able to name the game a ML model is…

items.title: Your Book Review: Orality and Literacy
items.excerpt: Imagine that you are dropped seven thousand years in the past, right in the middle of a village on a festival day. Everyone stares at you in horror: they think you’re a demon, a vengeful spirit. You are dressed in strange clothes, you are much taller than them, and you are holding a magic mirror that flashes with unexplained colors and sounds. The villagers are almost about to rush at you and kill you when the King’s right hand man, who happens to be visiting the village, comes to the front of the crowd. – State your business, demon . – I’m not a demon, I’m from the future. – If you’re really from the future, what gifts have you brought us? Oh shit. You don’t really have any gifts. You don’t know how to build an airplane, or how to make ammonia, or how to breed dwarf wheat. You think hard. Hmm… you do know one useful thing that, upon looking around, you are pretty sure these villagers don’t know. You tell the King’s right hand man what you know. He is pleased. He takes you with him to visit the King. You both arrive at court, and you sit on the sidelines as the right hand man goes up to the King to show off the new knowledge you gave him. As the King begins to speak, the right hand man demonstrates writing : IAMTHEKINGANDTHISISMYDECREE… Wait, what? 1. items.title: Your Book Review: The History And Adventures Of An Atom
items.excerpt: [ This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] I find, Gentlemen, when you read with me in private, that nine out of ten of you dislike the 18th century and all its literary works. As for the Women students, they one and all abominate it. — Arthur Quiller-Couch, “Of Selection” (1918) All eighteenth-century novels are weird in one way or another, if only because the novelists of the time didn’t yet know a standard by which to make them not-weird. Robinson Crusoe (1719) famously has no chapter breaks. Tristram Shandy (1767) famously contains a blank page, with instructions for readers to “call for pen and ink” and hack out a portrait of one of the characters on their own. The Man of Feeling (1771) is hardly a novel at all: An anonymous “editor” explains how a fat curate of his acquaintance had used torn pages from a small memorandum book as wadding paper while hunting; the few surviving pages of that memorandum, representing the scattered observations of an eccentric parishioner, make up the slim novel The Man of Feeling . It’s pretty weird. But one eighteenth-century novel is weirder than the rest. It is, in fact, by my estimation, weirder than any book written before Modernists of the twentieth-century started pushing the…

What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: Why Emery should stay at Aston Villa and reject Manchester United
items.excerpt: It was the kind of thinking that used to govern most of football. A few years ago – although it could really have been many examples from the last 50 – a promising manager was being pursued by one of the game’s wealthiest clubs. He had built up a fine team with an upwardly mobile club, and it looked like they could be on the brink of something special… but that one thought wouldn’t go away. “These opportunities don’t always come along, so you have to seize them.” The manager ended up taking it, but not quite seizing it. He didn’t perform to the level required, albeit amid a lot of debate around the circumstances he walked into. His career has never reached the same heights, but the key point is that its trajectory was, in that moment of acceptance, drastically changed. The old thinking was wrong. That job just wasn’t right for him. He’s not the only one. There are a few examples, from Graham Potter to Julen Lopetegui, and there’s much more to it than just “backing yourself”. items.title: Petrelintide Explained: The Long-Acting Amylin Analogue and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Petrelintide is a once-weekly peptide modeled on human amylin, a satiety hormone co-secreted with insulin. Zealand Pharma designed it; Roche and Genentech are co-developing it. This short covers how the amylin pathway differs from GLP-1 drugs, what the Phase 2 ZUPREME-1 trial showed on weight and cardiometabolic markers, the Phase 3 ZUPREME program now underway, and what trials reported on side effects, from mild nausea to placebo-like gut tolerability. items.title: Mazdutide Explained: The GLP-1 and Glucagon Dual Agonist and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Mazdutide is a once-weekly peptide modeled on oxyntomodulin that activates both the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. In 2025 China approved it for chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes, the first dual glucagon/GLP-1 agonist approved for weight loss. items.title: Elamipretide (SS-31) Explained: The Mitochondria-Targeting Peptide and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. In September 2025 the FDA granted it accelerated approval as Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome. This short covers how it works, what the TAZPOWER trial and its long-term extension showed, the mixed results in mitochondrial myopathy and dry macular degeneration, where the confirmatory and phase 3 trials stand, and what studies reported on side effects, from injection site reactions to allergic reactions and eosinophil changes. items.title: Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering
items.excerpt: This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year? Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption. As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub. Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.…

items.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
items.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.…

items.title: Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub
items.excerpt: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. items.title: Arnis turns any place on Earth into a Minecraft world
items.excerpt: Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it. I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet. Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors. Two weeks and a slow prototype Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school. That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow. Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with. You have until December 1, 2026, at 13:37 PST to build and submit a game inspired by SHIFT. Strong or loose inspirations apply! Join Game Off 2026 on itch.io shift /ʃɪft/ Noun A change in position, direction, perspective, or reality. A period of scheduled work, usually when something breaks. A keyboard key used to capitalize letters, sprint in games, and accidentally enable sticky keys. In computing, an operation that moves bits left or right, because apparently bits need exercise too. Amendments to the “Small Business” and “Small Organization” Definitions for Investment Companies and Investment Advisers for Purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act
items.excerpt: The Securities and Exchange Commission (the "Commission" or the "SEC") is amending the definitions of "small business" and "small organization" (collectively, "small entities") that are used in connection with Commission rulemaking under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (the "Investment Company Act") and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (the "Advisers Act"). These definitions concern regulatory requirements applicable to registered investment companies and business development companies (collectively, "funds") as well as investment advisers. The definitions are used specifically for purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (the "RFA"), which requires the Commission to consider the impact of its regulations on small entities. The amendments are designed to modernize the definitions, by increasing certain asset-based thresholds, including a mechanism for periodic future inflation adjustments, and eliminating the threshold based on total assets for advisers. In connection with these amendments, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV as well as the rule that allows certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a continuing hardship exemption from making Advisers Act filings electronically.

items.excerpt: This final rule with comment period revises the Medicare Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and the Medicare Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) payment system for calendar year 2027 based on our continuing experience with these systems. We also describe the changes to the amounts and factors used to determine the payment rates for Medicare services paid under the OPPS and those paid under the ASC payment systems. In addition, this final rule with comment period updates and refines the requirements for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and the Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Program. There are no changes to the Rural Emergency Hospital Quality Reporting Program. We finalized the expansion of the prior authorization requirement to include additional Botulinum Toxin Injection services. We also finalized implementation of certain provisions of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, for off-campus outpatient departments of a provider. In addition, this final rule with comment period announces notices of closure of teaching hospitals and opportunities to apply for available slots. Additionally, we finalized the policy that hospital accrediting organizations (AOs) with deeming authority may assess compliance with certain Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) administrative requirements under 42 CFR 489.20 during accreditation and reaccreditation surveys.

These truths are not at odds with one another, and being able to intellectually navigate both simultaneously and successfully requires a nuanced framework that has, in my opinion, failed to materialize thus far in the public conversation. The very idea of making an Artificial Intelligence lies within the combination of the intangible with the tangible — the conscious with the unconscious, the metaphysical with the physical, the spiritual with the worldly, the psychological with the physiological, etc. Today's AI programmers and chip manufacturers are yesterday's alchemists — attempting to turn sand into thought in lieu of lead into gold. An issue I find discussing AI is that the discourse so quickly sours to straight up propaganda from its creators or — perhaps more insidiously — surface-level, esoteric “mumbo jumbo” (see above) that muddies the ability to create informed consent for the masses. I have yet to resonate fully with any would-be sides of any would-be debate on the matter and remain quite skeptical of the public's perception on its implications today, not to mention tomorrow. items.title: The Praxian Genocidal Killchain - Part 4
items.excerpt: In Part 1, we defined the Praxians, considered their openly stated control of the Trump administration, and examined their extensive partnerships with the Israeli defence technology sector. In Part 2, we looked at State Crimes Against Democracy (SCADs) and Military-Civil Fusion within hybrid war. In Part 3, we examined how global forces have aligned behind the Praxian vision of a Network Empire as we move towards a UN 2.0 multipolar world. Now, in the concluding Part 4, we will see how all of this is coalescing in events playing out in the Middle East, how it is shaping global governance, and how, in microcosm, it is being applied to New Gaza. Across this entire series, we have explored the dawning of a new kind of global governance structure. We are heading toward a multipolar, regional balance of geopolitical power, where financial and economic power is wielded by those who program the nodes on the finternet—those who set the unified regulatory and financial architecture, irrespective of their geographical location. items.title: Scientists say this pesticide needs a warning label for pollinators
items.excerpt: Of the many chemicals humans have invented to control agricultural pests, some of the most devious are called “ insect growth regulators .” As the name suggests, these compounds don’t kill insects directly; they alter their development so they can’t grow into healthy, reproducing adults. This makes insect growth regulators a remarkably useful tool for taming populations of insects like whiteflies and mealybugs, which can spread diseases and sap nutrients out of food crops. There’s just one problem: Farmers don’t want to regulate all insects in this way. Beneficial insects like honey bees risk getting caught in the crosshairs of these chemicals, to the detriment of farmers who need their pollination services to produce crops like pears and cherries. One insect growth regulator in particular has emerged as a potential issue for pollinators: buprofezin. Ongoing research out of Washington State University, or WSU, suggests that buprofezin may be hazardous to honey bees even at concentrations 10 times below those commonly found in pollen. A study published in 2024 connected the compound to “severe brood mortality.” At a meeting of the Washington State Beekeeping Association last month, WSU entomology professor Brandon Hopkins said buprofezin products should be sold with a pollinator warning — a break from current requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA.
